title: FDA Approves First Drug Shown to Help Children With a Rare, Fatal Disease Live Longer
excerpt: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved Lembaz (adrabetadex) injection on Nov. 17, 2026 — the first treatment shown to help patients with infantile-onset
content:
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved Lembaz (adrabetadex) injection on Nov. 17, 2026 — the first treatment shown to help patients with infantile-onset Niemann-Pick disease type C live longer.

Niemann-Pick disease type C, known as NPC, is a rare, fatal genetic disorder in which cholesterol and other fats build up inside cells, damaging the brain and other organs. In the infantile-onset form, neurological symptoms begin before age 6.

The approval covers adults and children weighing at least 7 kilograms (about 15 pounds) with NPC whose neurological symptoms began before age 6, according to the FDA.

In the evidence the FDA relied on, treatment was associated with a 55% reduction in the risk of death compared with matched external controls. Median overall survival was 8.5 years for treated patients versus 4.9 years in the control group, according to the FDA and trade-press reports of the approval.

The evidence base was 36 patients with infantile-onset NPC treated across three clinical studies plus an expanded access program, compared with a matched external control group that the FDA deemed an adequate and well-controlled study.

Lembaz is given by intrathecal injection — into the spinal fluid — every two weeks by a trained provider.

The drug carries a boxed warning, the FDA's strongest, for hearing impairment, including permanent hearing loss — including in patients whose hearing was normal before treatment. Doses are adjusted based on repeated hearing tests. Ataxia and fatigue can occur in the days after each dose, according to the FDA.

Approval was granted to Mandos, LLC, a subsidiary of Beren Therapeutics of Thousand Oaks, California. The drug will be available at treatment sites nationwide in early December 2026, with a family access program to help coordinate treatment sites and out-of-pocket costs. Beren also received a Priority Review Voucher, and the drug had Breakthrough Therapy designation.

Lembaz is the first FDA-approved medicine to address the underlying cholesterol-trafficking defect that causes NPC, according to the company. An earlier survival analysis presented in March 2026, of 72 treated children versus 119 matched controls, reported a 71% lower risk of death and five-year survival of 84% versus 42%.

An important nuance: the approval rests on a comparison with matched external controls, not a randomized trial. The only randomized trial lasted 12 months, and its results led the FDA to rescind the drug's first Breakthrough Therapy designation, according to Contemporary Pediatrics. The company announcement did not report patient numbers, follow-up length or confidence intervals for the approval analysis.

This is the second NPC drug approval — the FDA approved a first NPC treatment on Sept. 20, 2024 — but Lembaz is the first shown to extend survival in the infantile-onset form.

This story is a news report, not medical advice. Lembaz is prescription-only and administered by trained providers; families affected by rare diseases in the 956 would access it through treatment sites nationwide starting in early December.
